name: Black-market / DIY fillers

lead: Black-market or DIY filler means dermal filler products people obtain outside licensed medical channels and use on their own faces. On looksmaxxing forums it is presented as a low-cost way to add structure to the jaw, chin or lips without visiting a clinic.

Fillers in general work by adding volume at the injection site, and hyaluronic acid gels of different firmness are used for structure or to soften transitions. The forum material consists of user guides and personal plans, not research. Published sources describe fillers given by trained providers, and no studies of self-injection were identified.

paras: Users describe sourcing products online and planning their own routines, mostly with hyaluronic acid-type gels. Details are left out here; people who want filler results can get the same product class through a licensed provider, who can also dissolve hyaluronic acid filler if needed.

Reference sources describe bruising, redness and pain as common, and rare but serious complications including blindness when material reaches the eye's arteries, usually permanent when it occurs. In the US, fillers are devices that a provider must inject. Forum posters themselves discuss vascular occlusion and nerve injury, and unregulated products have no quality checks.

chain: Self-injected into jaw, chin or lips
angle.text: People buy filler outside clinics and self-inject to add jaw, chin, cheek or lip structure cheaply, with the contour change visible straight away. Filler is well studied when clinicians give it; the self-injection practice rests on forum accounts.

lead: Black-market or DIY filler is the practice of buying injectable dermal filler outside regulated medical supply and administering it to oneself, as described on looksmaxxing forums. Participants describe it as a lower-cost route to the contour changes that clinics provide: more definition along the jaw, a more projected chin, or fuller lips, using gels of different firmness to add structure or soften transitions. It overlaps with the broader topic of unlicensed injection of fat-dissolving agents and botulinum toxin, which some users discuss in the same threads.

Reference sources state that in the United States dermal fillers are approved as medical devices and a provider must perform the injection, while in the UK and EU they are non-prescription devices under a CE mark that does not itself require proof of efficacy.[1] Wikipedia's overview lists bruising, redness and pain as common effects of fillers, infection and allergic reactions as less common, and blindness from embolisation into the retinal arteries as rare but typically permanent.[1] The US Food and Drug Administration's consumer page tells the public not to inject themselves and not to buy filler online, because products may be counterfeit or not approved for US use.[2]

Clinical literature on filler complications describes what can go wrong in any setting. A 2026 scoping review of 55 studies of facial hyaluronic acid injections, mostly case series and reports, listed bruising, ischemia and swelling as the most frequent reactions and tissue necrosis and embolism among the severe ones, some leading to blindness or stroke.[3] A Finnish registry study of 19 consumer complaints (2017 to 2024) found that unsuccessful lip filler was the most frequent issue and that 56 percent of cases occurred in beauty salons.[3]
No published study of self-injected filler was identified. Material about the practice comes almost entirely from forum posts, which this article describes only in general terms.

paras: On looksmax.org, threads on DIY filler include a long guide posted under a disclaimer that it neither promotes nor condones the practice, which lists the supplies, safety rules and warning signs its author considers essential. The guide distinguishes firmer fillers intended to add structure from softer ones intended to smooth transitions, and mentions microcannulas and hyaluronidase as tools to reduce risk or reverse hyaluronic acid filler. This article does not reproduce procedural details.

Other posters describe personal plans, for example a user who said he had ordered filler for the chin, a fat-dissolving product and botulinum toxin online and intended to study anatomy before self-injecting. A teenage poster asked whether jaw-widening filler would look unnatural as his face continued to grow.

Injectable fillers are substances placed in the skin and underlying tissue to restore volume or shape. Common materials include hyaluronic acid, collagen and poly-L-lactic acid, which are resorbed over time, and poly(methyl methacrylate), which is not. Hyaluronic acid fillers are often crosslinked with BDDE for stability, and Wikipedia notes questions about the long-term safety of that crosslinker.[1] Most wrinkle fillers are gradually metabolised and last about six months, and physical activity can shorten that.[1]

The FDA page states that approved absorbable fillers are indicated for adults aged 22 and over for wrinkles and for augmenting the lips, cheeks, chin and back of the hand, while non-absorbable fillers are approved only for nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars. Injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic use, and the agency lists the glabella, nose, area around the eyes, forehead and neck, as well as body contouring, among uses that are not approved.[2] Wikipedia counts six fillers approved in the US and more than 140 on the market in the UK and EU under CE marking.[1]

Wikipedia's dermal filler overview states that vision loss can follow injection when material travels back into the arteries supplying the eye, that it is usually permanent, and that delayed skin necrosis can occur [1]. It notes that fillers are not approved for some body areas [1].

Forum participants acknowledge risks as well: the guide mentions vascular occlusion and instructs readers to recognise its signs, and a reply in a separate thread about fat-dissolving injections warns that nerve damage is a risk that can outweigh the saving.

The FDA identifies injection into a blood vessel as the most serious risk, with possible tissue death, vision problems including blindness, and stroke; it adds that nodules, infection and allergic reactions are less common and that anaphylaxis, migration and death are rare. The page notes that removing filler can be difficult or impossible, especially with permanent products, and lists unusual pain, vision changes, or white, grey or blue skin near the injection site as reasons to seek immediate care.[2]

On supply, the agency's guidance says products bought online may be counterfeit or not approved for US use, and that injection should be treated as a medical procedure performed by a licensed provider with dermatology or plastic surgery experience.[2] Forum guides themselves discuss counterfeit concerns, hyaluronidase and microcannulas as ways posters try to manage risk, which is described here without procedural detail.

Published reviews describe the main outcomes plainly. A 2026 systematic search of PubMed from 2000 to 2024 on irreversible complications named blindness, stroke, chronic granulomatous inflammation and irreversible necrosis as the most severe, and reported that injection site, technique and filler permanence mattered more than volume alone; it states that hyaluronic acid fillers are preferred because they are reversible.[3] A review of vascular occlusion notes that aspiration is controversial and cannot reliably rule out intravascular placement.[3] A narrative review of cannula versus needle found cannulas associated with less bruising and a reduced signal for vascular occlusion in vessel-dense areas, but not risk-free, and warned that publication bias may underestimate complication rates.[3]

Management of an occlusion is a clinical matter. A scoping review of hyperbaric oxygen therapy covered 24 studies, mostly case reports and small series, and found low-level evidence because it was used alongside other treatments.[3] One 2026 case report describes a 29-year-old woman with nasal vascular occlusion after hyaluronic acid filler given by a non-medical injector, who needed repeated treatment and later had a stable scar with mild pigment change and surface irregularity at two years.[3]

Wikipedia's hyaluronic acid article adds that filler effects last about six to twelve months and that possible complications include nerve and microvessel injury, vascular occlusion and granulomatous foreign body reactions.[4]

Industry and training literature describes a rapid expansion of non-clinic injectors. A 2026 survey of 19,701 UK aesthetic practitioners across 5,589 clinics found practitioner numbers up 437 percent in two years and non-medical aestheticians rising from 12 to 24.8 percent of the workforce, with doctors at 28.4 percent.[3] A 2025 review argues that untrained providers pose patient safety risks and proposes a tiered training and certification model.[3]

The FDA says plainly that people should not inject themselves with dermal fillers or buy them online, and asks that problems be reported through its MedWatch system.[2] Danger signs it lists include unusual pain, vision changes, white, grey or blue skin near the injection site and stroke symptoms.[2]

Posters on appearance forums give cost, access and control as reasons: clinic filler is priced per syringe, appointments can be hard to get, and some users say they prefer to experiment with small changes gradually. Some say they study facial anatomy for weeks before planning anything. Others in the same threads advise using a clinic, citing nerve damage risk, and the community includes teenagers asking whether jaw filler would look unnatural as their faces continue to grow.
No studies found. Published reviews and trials of dermal fillers concern injection by trained clinicians.

Some forum users say they spent weeks studying facial anatomy before planning self-injection. Other forum users advise using a clinic, citing risks such as nerve damage. The community also contains minors asking about the practice.

The existence of threads, guides with disclaimers and requests for approval indicates a community conversation on cost, access and control; forum posts differ widely, and some advise professional care.

lore.intro: The practice is discussed on looksmax.org through how-to guides, shopping reports and requests for approval, sometimes with disclaimers distancing the author from encouraging it.
